title: C program structure, data types & input/output
overview: The first real module covers how a C file is laid out: comments, `#include`, `#define`, global declarations, `main`, and helper functions. It also covers the basic data types and the `printf`/`scanf` format specifiers that go with each type. Getting these right early saves many confusing bugs later.

concepts.term: Six sections of a C file
concepts.explain: Documentation comments, then `#include` lines, then `#define` macros, then global declarations, then `main`, then helper functions. Only `main` is required.
Lines starting with `#` run before compilation. `#include` pastes in a header file. `#define` does a plain find-and-replace.
A declaration like `int sum(int x, int y);` placed above `main` lets `main` call a function whose full body comes later in the file.
`short` has 2 bytes, `int` 4 bytes (about ±2.1×10^9), `long long` 8 bytes (about ±9.2×10^18), `char` 1 byte, `float` 4 bytes and `double` 8 bytes. Pick a type big enough for your largest value.
Each type has its own code: `%d` int, `%hd` short, `%lld` long long, `%c` char, `%f` float, `%lf` double. Using the wrong one gives garbage.

concepts.term: Reading a char after a number
concepts.explain: `%c` does not skip whitespace, so it may read the leftover newline. Write `" %c"` (with a leading space) to skip it.

files.title: Skeleton of a C program
files.what: An annotated outline of a C file's sections: comments, includes, defines, a global variable, a prototype, an empty `main`, and a `sum` function.
steps: Multi-line (`/* */`) and single-line (`//`) comments are ignored by the compiler.
`#include <stdio.h>` and `<math.h>` bring in the input/output and math libraries.
`#define pi 3.14` creates a constant by text replacement.
`int N = 100;` is a global variable, and `int sum(int x, int y);` is a prototype.
`main` just returns 0, and `sum` is defined after it.
files.output_note: The program prints nothing. It only shows the layout of a C file.
files.watch_out: `#define long long ll` is backwards: it makes a macro named `long`. It only compiles because nothing uses it. The intended line is `#define ll long long` (macro name first).

check.q: Why is the prototype `int sum(int x, int y);` needed if `sum` is written below `main`?
check.a: The compiler reads the file from top to bottom. The prototype tells it about `sum` before any call to it appears.

files.title: Program structure, fully explained
files.what: A polished version of basic.c. Each of the six sections has a comment block explaining it, and `main` now does something visible: it calls `sum` and uses `PI`, the `ll` macro and `sqrt`.
steps: `#define PI 3.1416` and `#define ll long long` are macros (text replacement, no memory used).
Global `N = 100` and the prototype of `sum` come before `main`.
`main` computes `sum(7, 5)`, `PI * N`, and `big = 10^9 * 10^9` stored in a `long long`.
Each result is printed with its matching specifier: `%d`, `%f`, `%lld`.

check.q: Why must `big` be a `long long` rather than an `int`?
check.a: 10^18 is far above the `int` limit of about 2.1×10^9. It fits only in 64 bits.

files.title: scanf / printf with many types
files.what: Reads several ints, a short, a char, a float and a double, then prints them back. It shows one format specifier for each type.
steps: `scanf("\n%c", &ch)` first skips the leftover newline, then reads one character.
`scanf("\n%.2f", &f)` is meant to read a float, but a precision like `.2` is not allowed in `scanf` (see Watch out).
The two `printf` calls print the values, including `e`, a short that was set to -32 in the code.
files.input_note: Line 1: three ints and a short. Line 2: a char. Line 3: a float. Line 4: a double.
files.output_note: The ints, the short and the char print correctly. But `f = 0.000000` and `g = 3.750000`: the float was never read, so its value is junk (here 0), and `3.75` went into `g`. The stray `\n, f =` appears because the newline is inside the first format string.
files.watch_out: `%.2f` is not valid in `scanf`, so the read stops and `f` stays uninitialized. Every later read shifts by one. Fix: `scanf("%f", &f);`. Use `.2` only in `printf`, like `printf("%.2f", f)`.

check.q: Which specifier reads a `short int` and which prints a `double`?
check.a: `%hd` reads a short. `%lf` (or `%f`) prints a double.

recap: A C file has six sections, and only `main` is required.
`#define` is text replacement: no type, no memory, no semicolon.
Choose the type by range: `int` goes to about 2×10^9, `long long` to about 9×10^18.
Match every variable with its specifier: `%d`, `%hd`, `%lld`, `%c`, `%f`, `%lf`.
Precision like `%.2f` is only for `printf`, never `scanf`.
Put a space before `%c` (`" %c"`) to skip leftover newlines.

check_yourself.q: Which type would you use for a value up to 10^15, and which specifier reads it?
What does `#define ll long long` do?
check_yourself.a: Before compiling, every `ll` in the code is replaced with `long long`.

check_yourself.q: Why can `scanf("%c", &ch)` read a newline by mistake after `scanf("%d", &n)`?
check_yourself.a: `%d` leaves the Enter key's newline behind, and `%c` does not skip whitespace. Use `" %c"` to skip it.
